claim: Acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured' is not met. Without a SurrogateType the collector always builds contractless members from every public read-write member of T. It never reads [MessagePackObject], [Key], [IgnoreMember], [DataContract] or [DataMember] on T. So a member marked [IgnoreMember] on T is still serialized, and [Key(n)] integer keys are replaced by string-name keys. The README and attribute docs in this change describe the same contractless-only behaviour.

claim: The change silently alters a security default unrelated to REQ-2129. MessagePackSecurity.GetHashCollisionResistantEqualityComparer used to throw TypeAccessException for types without a known hash-collision-resistant comparer. It now returns EqualityComparer<T>.Default. That removes hash-flooding protection for untrusted data on arbitrary key types.

The generated contractless formatter keeps only public read-write members, so public get-only properties and readonly fields are silently dropped from the serialized output. claim: The fallback in GetHashCollisionResistantEqualityComparer<T> now returns EqualityComparer<T>.Default instead of throwing TypeAccessException. Under MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData, a dictionary or set keyed by an arbitrary user type is deserialized with a non-collision-resistant comparer, so attacker-chosen keys can cause hash-flooding. This removes a security guard and is unrelated to REQ-2129.

claim: Contractless member collection ignores any MessagePack or DataContract attributes on T. When T carries [MessagePackObject] with [Key]/[IgnoreMember] (or [DataContract]/[DataMember]), the generated formatter still serializes every public read-write member under its name as a string key. An [IgnoreMember] property is therefore serialized and the [Key(0)] int keys are discarded. This breaks the acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured'.

claim: GetEqualityComparer fallback changed from throwing TypeAccessException to returning EqualityComparer<T>.Default. Existing users who relied on the exception, or on the secure-by-default behaviour, are affected without opting in.

claim: In contractless mode the generated string-key formatter emits members ordered by name, with IntKey set to the index. It excludes public get-only properties, readonly fields and init-only members, which ContractlessStandardResolver includes. A user who moves from the dynamic contractless resolver to this generated formatter would get a different wire map. The generated formatter is also opt-in, so the impact is limited to this feature.

claim: GetEqualityComparer<T> used to throw TypeAccessException for types with no known hash-resistant comparer when UntrustedData is active. It now returns EqualityComparer<T>.Default. This silently disables the collision-resistance protection: an attacker can send hash-colliding keys for any non-whitelisted key type (custom structs, classes) in Dictionary/HashSet and cause a hash-flooding DoS. The change is unrelated to the requirement and breaks a secure-by-default behavior.

claim: Surrogate mode lets string keys come from KeyAttribute, but the member-name match uses only the first member with that name. The new generated-formatter path reads and writes members without checking MsgPack-level restrictions on the target (for example, it gives no diagnostic for init-only or required members, and passes empty constructorParameters). A struct or class lacking a settable path could emit code that fails to compile or leaves required members unset. This is mainly a correctness risk, with a minor security impact from partially initialized objects.
